title: How Many Friends Can You Actually Keep Up With?
metaTitle: How Many Friends Can You Actually Keep Up With?
metaDescription: There is a rough ceiling on friendship. What Dunbar's research suggests about the layers of relationships you can realistically maintain — and why circles thin.
keyFinding: Research suggests humans can actively maintain only a limited number of relationships — very roughly around 150, arranged in nested layers — because each tie costs finite time and attention.
honestAnswer: Far fewer than most people assume, and that is normal rather than a failing. The influential proposal here is Robin Dunbar's, often called 'Dunbar's number': the suggestion that humans can sustain on the order of 150 stable relationships at once, with progressively smaller inner layers of closer ties. The figure is an approximation drawn from a particular line of research, not a hard biological limit — but the underlying point is well supported: maintaining a friendship takes time and attention, both of which are finite.

Because the supply is fixed, closeness in one layer comes at the expense of others. As life fills up with work, family, and obligations, the set of people you can genuinely keep up with tends to contract — and the people who drift out are not necessarily lost so much as moved to an outer layer. Treating your circle as something that should keep growing indefinitely runs against how the research suggests relationships actually work.
whatDataShows: Dunbar's work proposes that relationships sit in rough, nested layers rather than a single undifferentiated group. The commonly cited structure is approximately five intimate or closest people, around fifteen close friends, about fifty good friends, and roughly 150 meaningful contacts you would recognise and have a real relationship with — each outer layer including the ones inside it. These figures are averages with wide variation between people, not fixed quotas.

The mechanism Dunbar points to is finite capacity: there is a documented relationship between how much time you invest in a tie and how strong it stays. Closer relationships in the inner layers require disproportionately more contact and effort to maintain, which is part of why the inner circles are so small. When time is diverted elsewhere, ties tend to slide outward toward less demanding layers.

It is worth being honest that the exact '150' is contested and based on a specific body of work; some researchers question the precision of the number. What is less contested is the broader pattern the research describes — that meaningful relationships are layered, that closeness scales with invested time, and that total active capacity is limited rather than open-ended.
whyItFeelsDifferent: Modern life inflates the apparent size of your social world. Contact lists, follower counts, and group chats can hold thousands of names, which makes a shrinking set of people you actually talk to feel like a personal shortfall. But most of those connections sit far outside the layers Dunbar describes as active relationships — they are recognised contacts, not friendships you are maintaining.

There is also a strong cultural script that more friends is better and that a thinning circle signals something has gone wrong. The research suggests the opposite framing: a small number of close ties plus a wider ring of looser ones is roughly what capacity allows, and concentrating limited time on fewer people is often what keeps the inner layers strong.

And because everyone else's outer-layer contacts are visible while their actual close circle is not, other people can appear to be effortlessly maintaining huge networks. What you usually cannot see is that their genuinely active relationships are subject to the same finite ceiling as yours.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The most consistent implication is to spend your limited social time deliberately rather than evenly. Because closer ties decay without contact and require more upkeep than outer ones, the research points toward protecting regular contact with the inner layers rather than spreading thin attention across a very large group.

Accepting natural thinning as the system working, not breaking, also helps. As circumstances change, people move between layers; allowing an old friend to settle into an outer layer — staying in touch occasionally rather than feeling you have failed them — fits how capacity actually distributes across a life.

Where you want to bring someone into a closer layer, the lever the research highlights is invested time and contact, not intensity in a single moment. Strengthening a tie tends to mean repeated, ordinary contact over time, which is the same currency that maintaining the inner layers requires.
whatDoesNotHelp: Trying to maximise the raw number of friends tends not to help, because it spreads a fixed budget of time and attention more thinly and can weaken the inner ties that matter most. The layered model suggests breadth is naturally limited; pursuing it past your capacity comes at the cost of depth.

Treating large follower or contact counts as a measure of your social life is misleading. Those numbers sit well outside the active layers and say little about whether you have people you can actually keep up with — which is the thing the research is really about.

Guilt-driven attempts to keep every past friendship in the inner circle also tend to backfire, since there is simply not enough capacity for all of them to stay close at once. Holding every relationship to the same standard of contact usually strains the few that are genuinely closest.
realNumbersInContext: Dunbar's proposed layers are best read as rough averages, not targets: approximately 5 closest people, about 15 close friends, around 50 good friends, and roughly 150 meaningful contacts — each layer nested inside the next. Individuals vary widely around these figures, and the precise numbers are debated; the structure and the underlying constraint are the durable part.

The constraint behind the numbers is time. Research in this area links the strength of a relationship to the amount of contact it receives, with closer ties requiring disproportionately more. That is why the inner circle is small and why, as time gets scarcer, relationships tend to migrate toward the outer, lower-maintenance layers rather than disappear entirely.

faqs.question: Is Dunbar's number of 150 a hard limit?
faqs.answer: No. It is an approximation from a particular line of research, with wide individual variation and some scientific debate about its precision. The well-supported idea is not the exact figure but the pattern behind it: relationships are layered, closeness scales with invested time, and total active capacity is finite.

faqs.question: Why can't I keep up with all my friends anymore?
faqs.answer: Because maintaining a friendship costs time and attention, both of which are limited. As life fills with work and family, the research suggests ties naturally migrate to outer, lower-contact layers. Most of those friends are not lost; they have simply moved further out, which is how a finite social capacity tends to distribute.

faqs.question: How many close friends is normal to have?
faqs.answer: Dunbar's layers suggest roughly five in the closest, most intimate layer and around fifteen close friends, on average and with wide variation. These are descriptive estimates, not benchmarks to hit — having fewer is common and within the normal range.

faqs.question: Does having lots of online contacts mean I have lots of friends?
faqs.answer: Not really. Large contact and follower counts sit well outside the active relationship layers the research describes. They reflect recognised connections rather than friendships you are actively maintaining, so they say little about how many people you can genuinely keep up with.

faqs.question: Is it bad that my circle has gotten smaller?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. A thinning circle as life fills up is consistent with how finite social capacity works, not a sign of failure. The research even suggests concentrating limited time on fewer people is part of what keeps the closest ties strong.

dataSources: Robin Dunbar — research on 'Dunbar's number' and the layered structure of human relationships (roughly 5 / 15 / 50 / 150).
